newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian shares seen losing further ground.
newsitem.headline: Belgian shares seen losing further ground.

text.p: Belgian shares slipped with other European markets on Thursday, and dealers said the outlook for Friday remained bearish.
"It will probably be stable to negative," one trader said.
The Bel-20 leading share index, after trading in a tight range for most of the session around its Wednesday close, ended down 4.62 points, or 0.26 percent, at 1,765.13.

Disappointment at U.S. weekly jobless figures mid-afternoon at one point pushed the index down to 1,758.69 francs, but sustained buying of cement maker CBR and bank BBL helped the index pare its losses.
CBR was the most active stock for the second session in a row, rising 25 francs to 2,380 francs on trade in 289,266 shares linked to the expiry in December of a put warrant in its share.
Dealers attributed the volume to Germany's Heidelberger Zement, which issued the warrant in 1993 when it bought 42.4 percent of the company from Belgium's Societe Generale de Belgique.
Heidelberger announced mid-session via the Brussels Stock Exchange that it had raised its stake in CBR to over 50 percent, which it had consistently said was its long term goal.
"Heidelberger will do everything now to avoid receiving more shares...but I'm sure a lot of institutions will exercise the put if it's just above the strike price of 2,350 francs," one trader said.

He added that Heidelberger was stuck with the choice of trying to push up CBR's share, buy the warrants or even extend their expiry date, possibly by issuing a new warrant. With around 11 million shares outstanding the speculative atmosphere surrounding the share was likely to continue for some days.
BBL rose 170 francs, or 2.0 percent, to 6,530 in volume of 22,929 shares, but dealers could not explain the activity.
Most other Bel-20 issues were lower, hit by bond market weakness that followed the surprise fall in U.S. weekly jobless figures and a weak start on Wall Street.
SGB, which announced it had sold most of its shares in French oil group Elf for seven billion Belgian francs, ended down 25 francs at 2,365.

Retailer GIB slipped four francs to 1,294, unmoved by a sell-off of shares in hamburger unit Quick. Quick hit a 1996 low of 2,150 francs late in the day on a French parliamentary demand to increase the sales tax on fast food. The stock settled 175 francs, or 7.8 percent lower, at 2,190 francs.

The French parliament is not due to debate the budget proposal until next week, but dealers are already expecting it could go through. They say this would hit Quick, which has already been bruised this year from the mad cow crisis.

"The French government needs all the money it can get and I'm sure something is going to happen, especially when you consider that restaurants are already taxed at 20 percent," one trader said. "It's going to cost (Quick) a lot of money," he added, noting the company has two thirds of its sales in France.
It was too early to buy the shares, Generale Bank said in an investor note written after the news.
